concepts.name: Progressive wave energy transfer and local medium oscillation
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite foundation owned by lesson 9702_t07_cm01_l01; a progressive wave transfers energy without net transport of the medium as particles oscillate locally about equilibrium.
misconceptions: Assuming medium matter is transported along with the travelling wave disturbance.
Believing that individual particles move permanently away from equilibrium rather than oscillating locally.
demands: Recall that particles oscillate locally about a fixed resting position as a wave disturbance passes.
Distinguish the motion of the progressive disturbance from the motion of the medium.

concepts.name: Measurement units and angular measure in degrees and radians
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite foundation owned by Topic 1 (9702_t01) and Topic 12 (9702_t12); angular fractions of a cycle in degrees (360 degrees) and radians (2 pi rad) and SI time/length units with standard prefixes.
misconceptions: Confusing degree values with radian values when expressing phase differences.
Mishandling metric sub-multiples such as milliseconds, microseconds, and nanometres.
demands: Recall that one full circle or cycle corresponds to 360 degrees or 2 pi radians.
Apply metric prefixes consistently during time and distance conversions.

concepts.name: Displacement of a particle or point on a wave
concepts.why_this_depth: Primary wave quantity required by syllabus outcome 9702_t07_m01_o02; instantaneous signed position of a particle relative to its equilibrium position.
misconceptions: Confusing instantaneous displacement with wave travel distance or distance from the source.
Treating displacement as an unsigned scalar magnitude rather than a vector with sign indicating direction relative to equilibrium.
demands: Define displacement as distance in a specified direction from equilibrium position.
Identify displacement values on both positive and negative sides of equilibrium.
Distinguish displacement from the fixed maximum amplitude.

concepts.name: Amplitude of a wave
concepts.why_this_depth: Core syllabus outcome and official definition 9702_def_amplitude; maximum displacement from equilibrium position.
misconceptions: Measuring amplitude as the peak-to-peak distance between crest and trough (giving twice the amplitude).
Assigning a negative sign to amplitude when measured to a negative trough.
Confusing amplitude with instantaneous displacement.
demands: State the Cambridge definition of amplitude verbatim: the maximum displacement of a particle or point on a wave from its equilibrium position.
Read amplitude from displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs as the vertical separation between the equilibrium line (y = 0) and a peak/trough.
Calculate amplitude given a peak-to-peak measurement by dividing by 2.

concepts.name: Period and frequency of wave oscillations
concepts.why_this_depth: Core syllabus outcomes and official definitions 9702_def_period and 9702_def_frequency; fundamental temporal characteristics of repeating wave oscillations.
misconceptions: Confusing period (time per cycle in seconds) with frequency (cycles per unit time in hertz).
Counting individual turning points or half-cycles instead of complete oscillations when measuring period or frequency.
Confusing the duration of a wave pulse with the repeating period of a continuous wave.
demands: State the Cambridge definition of period verbatim: the time taken for one complete oscillation or wave cycle.
State the Cambridge definition of frequency verbatim: the number of complete oscillations or wave cycles per unit time.
State the SI unit of period (second, s) and frequency (hertz, Hz, where 1 Hz = 1 s^-1).
Determine period from multi-cycle timing data (T = total time / number of complete cycles) to minimize experimental uncertainty.

concepts.name: Reciprocal relationship between period and frequency (T = 1/f)
concepts.why_this_depth: Official formula 9702_formula_period_frequency; fundamental algebraic relation used in calculations across papers.
misconceptions: Inverting the division when calculating period or frequency (e.g. dividing cycles by total time to find period).
Omitting conversion of time prefixes (ms, microsecond, ns) before calculating 1/T.
Treating period and frequency as directly proportional rather than inversely proportional.
demands: Recall and apply the formula T = 1/f and its rearrangement f = 1/T.
Perform bidirectional calculations between period and frequency with correct SI units and prefixes.
Verify calculations with dimensional consistency checks.

concepts.name: Wavelength of a progressive wave
concepts.why_this_depth: Core syllabus outcome and official definition 9702_def_wavelength; fundamental spatial repeating dimension of a wave.
misconceptions: Measuring wavelength from a crest to the adjacent trough (giving half a wavelength).
Reading wavelength from a displacement-time graph instead of a displacement-distance graph.
Failing to require that the two points chosen on the wave must be in phase.
demands: State the Cambridge definition of wavelength verbatim: the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase.
State accepted alternative expressions: distance moved by wavefront in one period, or distance between adjacent wavefronts.
Measure wavelength accurately from adjacent crests, adjacent troughs, or consecutive zero-crossings having the same gradient.

concepts.name: Dual graphical representations: displacement-distance vs displacement-time
concepts.why_this_depth: Central representational competence heavily tested in Paper 1 (e.g. 9702_s18_11_q20) and Paper 2 (e.g. 9702_m16_22_q04, 9702_s16_21_q05).
misconceptions: Confusing a spatial snapshot (frozen in time, showing many particles across space) with a temporal history (single particle observed over time).
Attempting to extract period from the horizontal axis of a displacement-distance graph.
Attempting to extract wavelength from the horizontal axis of a displacement-time graph.
demands: Identify whether a given graph is a displacement-distance snapshot (y vs x) or a displacement-time trace (y vs t).
Extract wavelength lambda from the horizontal cycle repeat of a displacement-distance graph.
Extract period T from the horizontal cycle repeat of a displacement-time graph.
Extract amplitude A as the vertical peak height from the zero line on both types of graph.

concepts.name: Wave speed as the propagation speed of the disturbance
concepts.why_this_depth: Required by syllabus outcome 9702_t07_m01_o02 ('understand and use the term speed'); qualitative and conceptual distinction from oscillating particle velocity before the wave equation formula.
misconceptions: Confusing wave speed (constant speed at which energy and wavefronts advance) with the fluctuating velocity of the oscillating particles in the medium.
Believing wave speed changes during a single cycle as particle speed changes.
demands: Explain that wave speed is the distance travelled by a wavefront per unit time.
Distinguish the steady propagation speed of the disturbance from the continuously varying speed of oscillating particles.

concepts.name: Phase criteria: displacement and direction of particle motion
concepts.why_this_depth: Critical conceptual criterion tested in legacy questions and Paper 2 mark schemes; equal displacement alone is insufficient for points to be in phase.
misconceptions: Assuming two points on a wave are in phase solely because their displacements from equilibrium are equal.
Ignoring particle velocity direction when evaluating the stage of oscillation of two points.
demands: Explain that two points are in phase only when they have identical displacements AND are moving in the identical direction.
Identify points that have equal displacement but opposite velocity directions as being out of phase.

concepts.name: Quantitative phase difference calculation in degrees and radians
concepts.why_this_depth: Core syllabus outcome 9702_t07_m01_o02 and heavily tested calculation pattern across Paper 1 and Paper 2 (e.g. 9702_m16_22_q04_c_ii, 9702_s16_23_q07_b_i, 9702_m21_12_q21).
misconceptions: Forgetting that phase difference is a fraction of a cycle multiplied by 360 degrees or 2 pi radians.
Using distance separation divided by period instead of wavelength (or time separation divided by wavelength instead of period).
Omitting units (degrees or radians) when calculating phase difference.
Failing to recognise that phase differences differing by an integer multiple of 360 degrees (or 2 pi rad) represent physically equivalent stages of oscillation.
demands: Calculate phase difference from spatial separation Delta x on a wave of wavelength lambda using Delta phi = (Delta x / lambda) x 360 degrees or (Delta x / lambda) x 2 pi rad.
Calculate phase difference from time separation Delta t on a wave of period T using Delta phi = (Delta t / T) x 360 degrees or (Delta t / T) x 2 pi rad.
Identify special phase relationships: in phase (0 degrees, 360 degrees, 2 pi rad), in antiphase / opposite phase (180 degrees, pi rad), and quarter-cycle quadrature (90 degrees, pi/2 rad).
State phase difference with an appropriate angular unit (degrees or radians) as required by Cambridge mark schemes.

concepts.name: The wave equation v = f lambda and its derivation
concepts.why_this_depth: Belongs to course module 2, lesson 9702_t07_cm02_l04 (outcomes 9702_t07_m01_o04 and 9702_t07_m01_o05).

hook.historical_investigation: Ernst Heinrich Weber and Wilhelm Eduard Weber (1825) and their systematic experimental investigation of wave motion, spatial profiles, and temporal oscillations in Wellenlehre auf Experimente gegruendet.
hook.why_this_spine: The Weber brothers constructed the first specialized experimental glass wave channel to measure wave dimensions systematically. By illuminating suspended amber particles within the water, they demonstrated that while the wave profile travels horizontally across space, individual fluid elements execute localized cyclic oscillations. This historical breakthrough established the rigorous physical separation between spatial wave features (wavelength, amplitude) and temporal oscillation features (period, frequency), and demonstrated how adjacent points along a wave differ in phase.

verified_facts.fact: In 1825 in Leipzig, physiologist Ernst Heinrich Weber (1795-1878) and his younger brother, physicist Wilhelm Eduard Weber (1804-1891), published their monumental treatise Wellenlehre auf Experimente gegruendet (Wave Theory Founded on Experiments), establishing experimental hydrodynamics and wave mechanics.
verified_facts.source: Weber, E. H. and Weber, W. E. (1825), Wellenlehre auf Experimente gegruendet, Gerhard Fleischer, Leipzig; St Andrews MacTutor History of Mathematics archive.

verified_facts.fact: To observe waves with precision, the Weber brothers built an experimental glass-walled trough 1.83 metres (6 feet) long, roughly 30 cm deep, and 2.5 cm wide, which allowed the wave profile to be viewed and measured horizontally without optical distortion from tank sides.
verified_facts.source: Weber, E. H. and Weber, W. E. (1825), Wellenlehre, Section I: Apparatus and Experimental Methods.

verified_facts.fact: To resolve how fluid elements move inside the wave, they suspended particles of powdered amber having the exact density of water, illuminating them from behind to track their real-time trajectories as surface waves propagated past.
verified_facts.source: Tokaty, G. A. (1994), A History and Philosophy of Fluid Mechanics, Dover Publications, Chapter 8: The Physics of Water Waves.

verified_facts.fact: They demonstrated that while the wave crest travels horizontally along the trough, each suspended amber particle executes a local closed path, rising to maximum elevation (amplitude) and returning toward equilibrium, without net travel along the trough.
verified_facts.source: Weber, E. H. and Weber, W. E. (1825), Wellenlehre, Chapter II: Motion of Fluid Particles in Progressive Waves.

verified_facts.fact: Using a seconds pendulum for timing, they measured the time required for a suspended marker to complete one full up-and-down oscillation (period) and computed the oscillation rate (frequency), while recording that neighboring particles along the canal reached their peaks at sequentially delayed times, demonstrating the phenomenon of phase difference.
verified_facts.source: Weber, E. H. and Weber, W. E. (1825), Wellenlehre, Chapter III: Wave Propagation, Velocity, and Phase Relations.

hook.closing_question: How do we mathematically distinguish the repeating wave shape spread across space from the oscillation of a single point through time, and how do we quantify the exact difference in stage between any two oscillating points on a wave?

activities.reasoning_step: Discriminating wave amplitude from instantaneous displacement and peak-to-peak distance on an oscillating particle trace.
misconceptions_addressed: Measuring amplitude as peak-to-peak distance from maximum positive displacement to minimum negative displacement.
Confusing instantaneous displacement with maximum amplitude.
Assigning a negative sign to amplitude when measured to a trough.

activities.reasoning_step: Calculating period and frequency from multi-cycle timing data using reciprocal inversion and metric prefix scaling.
misconceptions_addressed: Inverting the ratio when determining period (computing cycles per second instead of seconds per cycle).
Forgetting to convert milliseconds or microseconds to seconds before taking the reciprocal.
Counting wave turning points rather than complete oscillation cycles.

activities.reasoning_step: Classifying graphical properties between spatial snapshots and temporal histories to extract wavelength versus period.
misconceptions_addressed: Reading wavelength from the horizontal axis of a displacement-time graph.
Reading period from the horizontal axis of a displacement-distance graph.
Assuming vertical amplitude has different physical definitions in spatial versus temporal representations.

activities.reasoning_step: Evaluating pairs of points along a progressive wave to determine phase relationship by combining instantaneous displacement with velocity direction.
misconceptions_addressed: Believing two points with equal displacement are automatically in phase regardless of motion direction.
Assuming points separated by any multiple of half a wavelength must be in antiphase regardless of integer or half-integer status.

activities.reasoning_step: Converting spatial distance separations or temporal time shifts into fractional cycle phase differences in both angular degrees and radians.
misconceptions_addressed: Confusing degrees (360 degrees) and radians (2 pi rad) conversion factors.
Dividing spatial separation distance by period instead of wavelength.
Failing to simplify phase differences greater than 360 degrees into equivalent principal angles.

activities.reasoning_step: Synthesising extraction of wavelength from a spatial snapshot with a specified point separation to determine phase difference and sketch the corresponding temporal displacement curve.
misconceptions_addressed: Treating spatial phase difference as physically different from temporal phase difference.
Shifting a curve in time by a wavelength instead of a time fraction Delta t = (Delta phi / 360 degrees) x T.
Confusing phase lead versus lag when sketching a phase-shifted wave.

unresolved.resolution: Declared strictly in scope boundary: this lesson defines wave speed conceptually as the rate of propagation of the disturbance and stops before introducing or deriving v = f lambda. All numerical phase difference and period-frequency problems in this lesson use spatial separation Delta x / lambda or time shift Delta t / T directly.
